q: A 2 kg ball moves at 3 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?
why: Ek = ½mv² = 0.5 × 2 × 3² = 9 J.

q: A 5 kg box is lifted 2 m. How much gravitational potential energy does it gain? (g = 9.8 N/kg)
A motor transfers 200 J of energy, of which 150 J is useful. What is its efficiency?
why: Efficiency = useful ÷ total = 150 ÷ 200 = 0.75 = 75%.

q: How does a lubricant reduce wasted energy in a machine?
c: It reduces friction between moving parts
why: Less friction means less energy dissipated as heat.

q: Which energy resource is renewable?
why: Wind is replenished as it is used; the others will run out.

q: What is a disadvantage of solar power?
c: It is not available at night and is less reliable in cloudy weather
why: Solar output depends on daylight and weather.

q: A 6 V supply drives 2 A through a resistor. What is its resistance?
How does the resistance of a thermistor change as its temperature rises?
why: An NTC thermistor's resistance falls as temperature increases.

q: Two 4 Ω resistors are connected in series. What is the total resistance?
why: In series, resistances add: 4 + 4 = 8 Ω.

q: In a parallel circuit, how is the potential difference across each branch related to the supply?
c: It is shared between the branches
It is the same as the supply
why: Each parallel branch has the full supply potential difference across it.

q: What is the potential difference of the UK mains supply?
why: UK mains is about 230 V a.c. at 50 Hz.

q: What colour is the earth wire in a UK plug?
why: Earth is green and yellow; live is brown; neutral is blue.

q: A 2 kW kettle runs for 60 s. How much energy is transferred?
Why does the National Grid transmit electricity at a very high potential difference?
c: It reduces the current, so less energy is lost heating the cables
It makes power stations more efficient
why: For the same power, higher p.d. means lower current and lower I²R losses.

q: A plastic rod rubbed with a cloth becomes negatively charged. What happened?
c: Electrons moved from the cloth to the rod
Electrons moved from the rod to the cloth
why: Only electrons move in static charging; the rod gained electrons.

q: Two negatively charged objects are brought close together. What happens?
why: Like charges repel.

q: A 2 kg block has a volume of 0.001 m³. What is its density?
What happens to mass when ice melts?
why: A change of state is a physical change; mass is conserved.

q: While water is boiling, its temperature stays at 100 °C. Where is the energy going?
c: Increasing the kinetic energy of the particles
Breaking the bonds between particles (increasing internal potential energy)
why: Latent heat changes the state without changing the temperature.

q: What is the specific latent heat of a substance?
c: Energy to change the state of 1 kg with no change in temperature
The temperature at which it boils
why: Specific latent heat is the energy per kilogram to change state.

q: Why does the pressure of a gas in a sealed container increase when it is heated?
c: Particles move faster and hit the walls harder and more often
why: Faster particles collide with the walls more often and with more force.

q: At constant temperature, a gas is compressed to half its volume. What happens to its pressure?
why: pV is constant at fixed temperature, so halving V doubles p.

q: What is an isotope?
c: An atom with a different number of protons
An atom of the same element with a different number of neutrons
why: Isotopes have the same protons (same element) but different neutrons.

q: Which model of the atom came first?
why: Thomson's plum pudding model was replaced after Rutherford's alpha scattering experiment.

q: Which type of radiation is the most ionising?
why: Alpha particles are the most ionising and the least penetrating.

q: A sample's activity falls from 800 Bq to 200 Bq in 6 hours. What is its half-life?
why: 800 → 400 → 200 is two half-lives in 6 hours, so one half-life is 3 hours.

q: Why is a gamma emitter used as a medical tracer inside the body rather than an alpha emitter?
c: Gamma passes out of the body to be detected and is less ionising
why: Gamma rays escape the body to a detector and cause less ionisation damage.

q: Which is a natural source of background radiation?
c: Rocks such as granite releasing radon
why: Radon from rocks and cosmic rays are natural sources.

q: What happens in nuclear fission?
c: A large nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei, releasing neutrons and energy
why: Fission splits a heavy nucleus such as uranium-235; the neutrons released can cause a chain reaction.

q: Where does nuclear fusion happen naturally?
why: Stars release energy by fusing light nuclei such as hydrogen.

q: Which quantity is a vector?
why: Velocity has size and direction; speed only has size.

q: What is the weight of a 50 kg person on Earth? (g = 9.8 N/kg)
A force of 10 N pushes a box 3 m. How much work is done?
What is 1 joule equal to?
why: 1 J of work is done when 1 N moves through 1 m.

q: A spring has a spring constant of 50 N/m. What force stretches it by 0.1 m?
What does it mean if a spring has passed its limit of proportionality?
c: Extension is no longer proportional to force
It returns to its original length
why: Beyond this limit, F = ke no longer applies.

q: A 20 N force acts 0.5 m from a pivot. What is the moment?
When is a beam balanced?
c: When the forces are equal on both sides
When clockwise moments equal anticlockwise moments
When the pivot is at one end
why: This is the principle of moments.

q: Why does pressure in a liquid increase with depth?
c: There is a greater weight of liquid above
why: More liquid above pushes down with more weight.

q: Why does atmospheric pressure decrease with height?
c: There is less air above, so less weight of air pushing down
Gravity is weaker at sea level
why: Higher up, there is less air above you and the air is less dense.

q: A car speeds up from 0 to 20 m/s in 5 s. What is its acceleration?
What does the gradient of a distance–time graph show?
why: Gradient = distance ÷ time = speed.

q: What is the momentum of a 1000 kg car moving at 20 m/s?
Why do car crumple zones reduce injury?
c: They increase the force on passengers
They increase the time taken to stop, reducing the force
why: Force = rate of change of momentum; a longer stopping time means a smaller force.

q: A wave has a frequency of 5 Hz and a wavelength of 2 m. What is its speed?
Which is a longitudinal wave?
why: Sound vibrations are parallel to the direction of travel.

q: Which electromagnetic wave has the shortest wavelength?
why: Gamma rays have the shortest wavelength and highest frequency.

q: Which electromagnetic waves are used for communicating with satellites?
why: Microwaves pass through the atmosphere and are used for satellite communication.

q: What is a perfect black body?
c: An object that reflects all radiation
An object that absorbs all radiation that hits it
An object that emits no radiation
why: A perfect black body absorbs all incident radiation and is also the best emitter.

q: An object is at a constant temperature. What is true?
c: It absorbs radiation at the same rate as it emits it
why: Constant temperature means absorption and emission are balanced.

q: What is an induced magnet?
c: A magnet that is always magnetic
A material that becomes magnetic only when in a magnetic field
why: Induced magnets lose most of their magnetism when removed from the field and always attract.

q: Which way do magnetic field lines point outside a magnet?
why: Field lines go from the north pole to the south pole.

q: A wire of length 0.5 m carries 2 A at right angles to a 0.3 T field. What is the force?
How can the strength of an electromagnet be increased?
c: Increase the current or add an iron core
why: More current, more turns or an iron core strengthen the field.

q: A transformer has 100 turns on the primary and 500 on the secondary. The primary p.d. is 10 V. What is the secondary p.d.?
why: Vs ÷ Vp = Ns ÷ Np, so Vs = 10 × 500 ÷ 100 = 50 V.

q: What does a dynamo produce?
why: A dynamo uses a split-ring commutator to produce d.c.; an alternator produces a.c.

q: What force keeps a satellite in orbit?
why: Gravity provides the centripetal force for circular orbits.

q: What is the next stage after a main sequence star like the Sun?
why: Sun-sized stars become red giants, then white dwarfs.

q: What does red-shift from distant galaxies show?
c: Galaxies are moving away from us, and the universe is expanding
why: The further away a galaxy, the greater its red-shift, so it is receding faster.

q: Which theory does red-shift support?
why: An expanding universe suggests it began from a very small, hot region.
